The word kickback has two completely separate meanings — one involving money and corruption, and one involving physical force. Both are widely used, so you need to understand both. The financial/corruption meaning is by far the more common and important one.

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in news, business, law, and everyday conversation.

A kickback is a sum of money secretly paid to a person in return for helping someone else get a business deal, contract, job, or other benefit — especially when that help involves the person abusing their position of power or trust.

A simple way to picture it

Imagine a government official whose job is to decide which construction company gets a big contract to build a new highway. Company A really wants that contract. So instead of competing fairly, they secretly hand the official a large amount of money "under the table." In exchange, the official makes sure Company A gets selected. That secret payment is the kickback.

The logic of the word makes intuitive sense: a portion of the money from the deal gets "kicked back" to the person who made the deal happen in the first place.

The essential characteristics of a kickback

A kickback is always secret. If the payment were openly declared, it would just be a commission or a fee. The secrecy is what makes it a kickback.

A kickback is almost always illegal. It is treated as a form of bribery and corruption in most countries. Both the person who pays the kickback and the person who receives it are typically committing a crime.

A kickback involves a person in a position of power. The receiver of the kickback is usually someone who has the authority to make a decision that benefits the payer — awarding a contract, approving a purchase, granting a license, choosing a supplier, etc.

A kickback usually involves a percentage of the deal's value. If a supplier wins a $1 million government contract and secretly gives the approving official $100,000, that $100,000 is the kickback — effectively 10% of the deal "kicked back" to the decision-maker.

Common places where kickbacks happen

Kickbacks are most associated with government and public contracting (officials who award public projects), healthcare (doctors or hospital administrators paid by pharmaceutical or medical equipment companies to prefer their products), corporate procurement (a company's purchasing manager secretly paid by a vendor to keep buying from them), and construction and real estate. Anywhere that someone has the power to steer a decision toward a specific party, kickback schemes can exist.

Example sentences

  • "The senator was charged with accepting kickbacks from defense contractors."
  • "The hospital's procurement officer had been receiving kickbacks from a medical supply company for years."
  • "Three executives were fired after an audit uncovered a kickback scheme involving their main supplier."
Meaning 2: A Sudden, Violent Backward Jolt from a Machine

This meaning is entirely physical and has nothing to do with money. A kickback here refers to the sudden, forceful, and often dangerous backward movement that a machine, tool, or firearm produces — usually unexpectedly — during operation.

A simple way to picture it

Imagine you are cutting a log with a chainsaw. If the tip of the blade catches the wood at the wrong angle, the saw can instantly and violently snap back toward your face or body. That dangerous, uncontrolled backward lunge is a kickback.

This meaning is especially important in the context of power tools (chainsaws, circular saws, table saws), where kickback is one of the leading causes of serious injury. It is also used for firearms, where the gun pushes sharply backward against the shooter's hands or shoulder when fired (though for guns, the word "recoil" is more commonly used). The word also applies to engines and other heavy machinery.

Example sentences

  • "The woodworker's hand was severely injured by a kickback from the table saw."
  • "Always wear protective gear and maintain a firm grip to prevent chainsaw kickback."
  • "Kickback injuries from power tools send thousands of people to the emergency room every year."
A Less Common, More Neutral Financial Use

Occasionally, you will hear "kickback" used in a relatively neutral financial sense to mean a portion of money returned to someone as part of a business arrangement — similar to a rebate or a commission.

For example: "Sales agents earn a kickback of 5% on every deal they close."

However, even in this neutral use, the word "kickback" carries a slightly informal and suspicious tone. In professional or formal writing, people prefer cleaner words like commission, rebate, or incentive. Whenever you see "kickback" in a financial context, there is almost always at least a hint of something shady being implied, even if not stated outright.
How to Tell the Two Main Meanings Apart

Context makes it almost impossible to confuse them:

If the sentence involves money, business, government, contracts, or corruption → it is the bribery/illegal payment meaning.

If the sentence involves a tool, a machine, a weapon, or a physical action → it is the sudden backward jolt meaning.

Kickback as a noun has two core meanings:

The primary and most important meaning is a secret, illegal payment made to a person in a position of power in exchange for a favorable decision — a form of bribery and corruption used to rig business deals, contracts, and more. Both giving and receiving kickbacks is typically a crime.

The secondary meaning is a sudden, violent, and dangerous backward recoil produced by a power tool, machine, or firearm during operation — a major safety hazard in settings like woodworking, construction, and forestry.

A third, minor use exists in neutral business language to mean a financial return or commission, but this use is informal and always carries an undercurrent of suspicion.
